newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian oil firms seek investments to meet demand.
newsitem.headline: Indian oil firms seek investments to meet demand.

text.p: A global conference between oil consumers and producers has provided a shop window to Indian oil firms seeking investments to meet the country's fast-growing energy needs, officials said on Sunday.

Heads of at least 14 Indian oil firms have been in the Indian beach resort of Goa for the past three days, touting the country's strong demand forecasts and looking for investments from oil-rich nations in refineries, pipelines and infrastructure.

The conference, which brings oil importers and exporters together, has given Indian oil companies a chance to display their potential to world oil producers hungry for more markets for their oil and gas.
"You admire this place, now invest in it," said a billboard on the road from the airport to the beautiful beach resort, making clear India's intentions on seeking a steady flow of funds.
The meeting, due to end on Sunday, is taking place against the background of the highest oil prices in almost six years.
India, struggling to handle a rising oil import bill, is emphasising security of supplies in the hydrocarbon sector and appropriate technology to continue exploration and production.
"The producers are looking for supplies to India. It is a high growth area," said Bikash Bora, chairman of Oil and Natural Gas Corp (ONGC) India's giant oil firm.

India's demand for petroleum products is expected to grow by more than six percent per year, doubling from the current level of 75 million tonnes to 150 million tonnes in the year 2010. The strong growth will require additional investment of $100 billion.
Frequent power breakdowns at the venue of the conference, that started with a Hindu prayer to fire and energy, highlighted India's fragile distribution network and poor infrastructure.

While no major deals have been signed during the conference, officials said the bilateral meetings between Indian oil executives and representatives from Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, Iran, Qatar, Indonesia and Brazil have laid the foundations for future cooperation.
"This meeting is a pace setter. You cannot be talking on nuts and bolts," said R. K. Narang, chairman of the Indian Oil Corporation (IOC).

India has ambitious plans to nearly double its refining capacity of about 110 million tonnes by 2010 from about 60 million tonnes now. Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil producer, is studying a joint venture project in Punjab and other countries, including Malaysia, are mulling projects elsewhere.
Distribution infrastructure like cross-country pipelines, port terminals and tankages will also be needed on a massive scale, Indian officials said.
Under a liberalised economic policy since 1991, the entire petroleum sector has been opened up for private participation for investments through joint ventures and strategic alliances.
Major companies like Shell, Amoco, Chevron, BHP and Enron are engaged in exploration for oil and gas. India's current production cannot meet even half of its needs.
The chairman of Oil India Ltd, N.N. Gogoi, said India was looking for capital for exploration activity in deep seas and geologically difficult areas.
"India has a net deficit. This deficit cannot be met just by wishful thinking, we have to have a lot of technology put in," Gogoi said.
Bora said India wanted to begin deep seas exploration next year and Brazil could provide its cost-effective technology for it.
Officials said India was looking for liquified natural gas from Iran, Qatar and Malaysia and more investments in joint ventures from Malaysia, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.
